items.note: Story 1: Association named, organized at Larrow Green 1889, Gideon Vose first president, creamery built 1891.
Story 1: paid by pounds of butterfat ascertained by test, not by weight; quotes 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern'.

Story 1 ties Article VII to what a man is paid and calls it 'the hinge of the whole matter'; Story 2 states that on payment by test small differences compound to money. Counterfactual not spelled out but the gating clause is met.
Effie Loomis and Hobart Sill appear nowhere in Section A (Loomis only in B3, Sill only in D2/F). Wilbur Teague named, but the item needs all three officers.
Section A gives Selby Vose as manager from 1913 but never states he was Gideon's son. The son relation is stated only in B3/E5 and credit does not travel into Section A.

Section A's only station-gain mention is inside the Bulletin 471 quotation, which is the 76,000 lb identity scored at A8.6. No statement of the line's 1898 origin, its ~5.25% shape, or its mechanism inside Section A.
Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up the valley, opened 4 May 1896. Borrowed-glass detail is only in Section F, but the item's core fact is present.
Story 1 describes weighing, sampling, cream shipped to Larrow Green, skim returned; Story 4 describes the pipette drawing the exact charge into the test bottle.
Ammon & Sons invoice 14 April 1897; equipment in use 1 May 1897; Tarnet named (Story 4 and the crate stencil in Story 5).
6 dozen / 72 pipettes at $77.93 (Story 1); marked 17.6 c.c. (Story 7).

Section A never states the station's shortfall was flat at 0.19 in every month across twenty-six years. Story 2's 'gap consistent year-round' is offered as a 0.17-0.19 range for the Hollow-vs-Green gap, not as the instrument signature.
Story 5 establishes that a pipette can only be checked against a calibrated burette, that the state began issuing them in 1921, and that most plants had never had their glass checked.
Ansel Keddie, tester from the station's 1896 opening, twenty-nine seasons, dismissed 30 April 1925; died 1934.
Test book named repeatedly, kept in his own hand across twenty-nine seasons; bench-routine detail absent but unbolded.
The summary leaf never appears in Section A. The 1896-on-borrowed-glass average of 3.80 is stated only in Section F; Section A's 3.80 figures are the 1911 interval and the post-1923 average.
Story 4: broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, ran 3.80, back to 3.61 the same day, question mark quoted.
Story 3: Orra was Emmet Brant's sister; Emmet the largest patron; the rupture spelled out.
1919 water circular over the manager's signature (Story 3); Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement, tested as he was taught, cannot say why, never took a pound of cream (Story 6).
Died 1934 (Story 8); test book to Ordell County Historical Rooms 1959.
Hessel Bottom the wet meadow; six farms; Emmet Brant's the largest.
Section A names Brant's weigh book only as an exhibit and an accession. No 1 January 1897 start, and no statement that his scale and the station's agreed.

1902 complaints correctly dated, but the run states the Hollow-vs-Green comparison as 0.19 (Story 3 '0.19-point persistent gap'; Section G 'lower than milk elsewhere - a gap of roughly 0.19'; Story 2 gives '0.17-0.19' for 3.61 vs 3.78). The key voids this item for that conflation.
Grigg committee, sampled January-March 1908, hay conclusion quoted as the committee's finding and later defeated in F4.
Brant's 1910 (200,000 lb at 3.42) appears only in C2. Nothing in Section A on proportionality or the richer herds losing more.
Story 8: weigh book lent by Roy Brant to Ivy, then Hazel Brant.

Section A has no Alder Corners story at all. Story 8 mentions only 'the Alder Corners test book' passing from Jerome Cudd to Rosalie to the Vessey County Historical Society. No cheese company, no Redlow Ridge.
The four Hessel Bottom patrons hauling over the ridge in the summer flush from 1915 appears only in Section F.
The independence of the Alder Corners test is never argued in Section A.
The 0.19 differential across sixteen overlapping seasons is absent from Section A (Section F cites only a 3.79-3.82 range).
What the comparison disposes of is argued only in Section F.
Rosalie correctly given as Jerome's daughter, but Section A never connects her to Ivy or to the sixteen seasons of figures copied out in 1958.
Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector for the Ordell circuit since 1907 (Story 5); notebooks to the state office in 1936 (Story 8).
Story 5 lists the lactometer as part of his routine but never states he never once found added water at Ostrey Hollow. That claim appears only in Sections E and F.
12 June 1923, pipettes run against the burette, whole lot condemned.
No statement that Strawn wrote no figure for the deficiency or made no report beyond the condemnation. 'No person at the time made any connection' is a different claim.
Ordered 28 June, answered 2 July, in use the following month, 1924 average 3.80 and stayed there, and nobody connected the rise with the condemnation.
Crate to the loft over the intake room; notebooks to the state office 1936 then Farland 1947 where Ivy found the 1923 volume.
January 1925 petition.
Board under Alonzo Frick, three sessions, first at Ashlin 17 March 1925, second and third in the station's weigh room, award 4 May 1925.
Water (Vose), theft (Teague), hay (1908 report revived); 'found no cause established'.
Four exhibits listed correctly, including the state inspector's notebook.
Dismissed 30 April 1925 before any finding; award 4 May 1925 of $3,800 'without admission' charged to the station account.
States the loss as $19,600 (a planted error, deducted separately) and never connects the award's account to the station-gain account that had been accumulating the loss since 1898.
Ivy Keddie, granddaughter, graduate student in dairy husbandry at Farland, Professor Leland Vaught named.

Section A shows her drawing on Strawn's 1923 notebook (unread at Farland since 1947), Brant's weigh book lent by Roy, the Association's ledgers and the crate. The Alder Corners figures are missing but the assembly of dispersed records is present.
February 1958, crate in the station loft, nine pipettes surviving.
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, nine readings listed, mean 16.72 against a marked 17.6, short 0.88 c.c., 95 hundredths of the mark.
Bulletin quote covers 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 at one part in twenty; Story 7 gives 3.61 recorded against a true 3.80; 0.19 stated elsewhere in Section A.
REQUIRED four all present and right: 40,000,000 lb milk, 76,000 lb fat, $19,000 at 25 cents, and the ledger identity in the Bulletin 471 quotation.

Bulletin No. 471, October 1958 correct, but the intervals are wrong: Story 8's Quantities give '24-year gap between dismissal and vindication' (should be 33) and '34-year gap between Ansel's death and vindication' (should be 24), contradicting its own prose.
Granddaughter, with the full derivation through Duncan, and the great-niece error identified and corrected.
Second cousins with a correct derivation (+1). Abstention half lost: the run asserts sibling status flatly at B2 and resolves the full/half question at E8 as 'Full sister is more likely correct'.
Gideon Vose, his father (+1); significance correctly tied to Gideon's authorship of Article VII making the station's test decide pay (+1).

Abstention half lost: headline verdict 'there was no family connection between the Vose and Keddie families' and 'the persistent valley rumor was baseless'; the later 'cannot entirely settle this' does not undo it. Second point earned for laying out the poles correctly (Toland and Oram from talk, Duncan's flat denial).
States 95 percent / one part in twenty / 5 percent short, despite an erroneous intermediate ratio of 0.9477.
Carries the bad 0.9477 forward: answers 3.806 percent 'call it 3.81' and a shortfall of 0.20 points, offering 0.19 only as 'the commonly cited' figure. Key requires 3.80 and 0.19 exactly.
$19,000 at 25 cents; $3,800 received; 20 percent, one fifth. Both money and fraction given.
$90.00 using $0.25 without stating that it is deliberately using the period average rather than the 1910 price of 24 cents. Key answer is $86.40.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb delivered.
Both denominators named: 5.00 percent of fat delivered, 5.26 percent of fat credited. Avoids the NT-20 trap.
$77.93. Line items not re-added, but the total is right and the $77.39 decoy is rejected.
72 pipettes (6 dozen), each short 0.88 c.c.
26 years 1 month 11 days in use; 25 full delivery years 1898-1922; part-year reason given for the difference.
Abstention item A02 asserted: 'Approximately 900,000 pounds', taking Oram's memory as settled.
The pipette named as the one variable that changed.
Eight constants listed: patrons, herds, pasture, season, acid, bottles, hand tester, operator.
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 on 10 July.

States what it establishes (instrument, not milk, ground, tester or season) and states a limit (it does not by itself prove the glass caused the whole 26-year pattern). Not one of the key's three named limits, but a genuine limit is stated.
Three reasons from three narrators: Sill's heavy cream (R14), the 1911 interval (R4/R11), Teague's invariant ledger gain (R5).

Independence argued explicitly, and D1 states the 1911 interval 'would hold even if the glass had never been measured in 1958'. Reasons 1 and 3 do lean on the same underlying surplus, but they rest on different books and witnesses.
Abstention item A09 asserted: 'Did Teague question the entries? Yes.' Takes Teague's own account at face value with no mention of the clerk's contradiction or the absence of any minute.
Answers the literal question yes, citing the 1919 circular and the 1926 address.
REQUIRED three of five: manager from 1913, signed the annual ledger sheets carrying the station-gain line, wrote the 1919 circular, argued watering at the 1925 hearing.

Abstention item A03 asserted rather than declined: 'Vose knew the figures were anomalous', 'This suggests Vose knew the account was anomalous but chose not to investigate' - the station-gain line taken as proof of his knowledge.

Capped. Several conflicts found, correctly resolved, with a method stated: five dozen vs 6 dozen (invoice), 16.27 vs 16.72 (arithmetic on the primary data), nephew vs son (multiple correcting sources), $3,500 vs $3,800 (board record), 1921 vs 12 June 1923 (Strawn's contemporaneous notebook). None of the key's sixteen E-a table rows is flagged as a conflict, but each of these counts at E-a per the key's 'right value without noticing the pair' clause.

Only NT-18 breaks a pair: the run notes both R19 and R22 carried 'great-niece' and names the breakers (Duncan's family record, R22's own correction). NT-1, NT-15, NT-17 are each pinned on a single narrator; on NT-9 the run explicitly and wrongly declares 'No second narrator repeated this error'.
No abstention conflict handled. A04 never mentioned; A06 asserted as 'a borrowed measure from the creamery at Larrow Green'; A10 asserted as 'adopted at the annual meeting of 1892'.
Explicitly forfeited: 'Cases where a narrator contradicts itself: None found. Each retelling is internally consistent within its own section.' Nine such cases exist in the corpus.

Names the 1897 crate's pipettes at 16.72 against 17.6, calls the error proportional rather than additive, and gives both onset (1896 borrowed glass at 3.80, crate in use May 1897) and cessation (12 June 1923, 1924 at 3.80) with nothing on the farms changing.
Watering named to Selby Vose and defeated with Strawn's lactometer visits, the 1911 interval, and the Alder Corners figures.
Theft named to Teague and defeated with Sill's heavy cream, the 1911 interval under the same tester, and the invariance of the ledger gain.
Bog hay named to the 1908 committee and defeated with Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer, the Alder Corners comparison, and Falke's withdrawal.
Abstention item A07 asserted: answers the glassware question with a flat 'No.' before citing the evidence that merely leans that way.

Abstention item A05 asserted: 'Ansel Keddie believed water was being added by the patrons', then incoherently 'he suspected the glass but believed the patrons were adding water'. Treats Frick's and Duncan's uncorroborated recollections as settled.
About 183 words against a 150-word cap.
Names only the 1958 measurement. 'The remaining records were scattered across three counties' names no series; the arbitration is mentioned as an event, not a record.
All three decoys presented as explanations that circulated, not as fact, and no wrong headline number appears (uses $3,800, 5 percent, 95 percent, 26 years).
Only two of the six arc elements: the 5 percent / one part in twenty shortfall, and 1958. No 1897, no 76,000 lb or $19,000, no 1923 condemnation, and Ansel Keddie is never named. Four required.

Corruption: asserts Strawn's circuit/lactometer record beginning in 1908 - 'circuit notebooks (1908-1923)' in Story 3 and 'on every visit from 1908 onward' in Sections E and F - contradicting its own correct 1907 in Story 5
Gullibility A01: asserts there was no Vose-Keddie family connection and that the rumor was baseless (B4)
Gullibility A02: asserts the 1896 intake as approximately 900,000 lb (C5b and Story 1)
Gullibility A03: asserts Vose knew the account/figures were anomalous and chose not to investigate (D3)
Gullibility A05: asserts Ansel Keddie believed water was being added (F6)
Gullibility A06: asserts the 1911 measure was borrowed from the Larrow Green creamery (Story 4, D1, F2)
Gullibility A07: asserts flatly 'No' that the 1925 board examined the condemned glassware (F5)
Gullibility A08: asserts 'Full sister is more likely correct' for Orra and Emmet (E8)
Gullibility A09: asserts 'Yes' that Teague questioned the entries, on Teague's own say-so (D2)
Gullibility A10: asserts Article VII was adopted at the annual meeting of 1892 (Story 1)
